L23@P2: A Quarter-Century of Cybercrime Reporting
L24@P2: In 2025, the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) celebrated its 25th anniversary as
L25@P2: the central hub for reporting cyber-enabled crime. This milestone signifies the FBI's
L26@P2: enduring commitment to fighting the ever-evolving cyber threat. Our success in protecting
L27@P2: individuals and organizations is driven by public participation and robust data analysis.
L28@P2: For the past quarter-century, IC3 has been the primary connection between the FBI and the
L29@P2: public for information related to cyber-enabled criminal activity. Since our founding,
L30@P2: reporting to IC3 has surged. We received a few thousand complaints per month in our early
L31@P2: days. We now average almost 3,000 complaints per day. IC3 produces annual reports (like
L32@P2: the one you are reading) based on the information we receive, publishes public awareness
L33@P2: campaigns, and provides industry alerts to the private sector. IC3 remains an essential
L34@P2: resource for our law enforcement colleagues in combating cyber-enabled crime.
L35@P2: In 2025, losses reported to IC3 continued to climb, surpassing the $20 billion mark.
L36@P2: Investment-related fraud was once again the largest component of these losses, followed
L37@P2: by business email compromises and tech support scams. The FBI continues to disrupt and
L38@P2: deter malicious cyber actors -- and shift the cost from victims to our adversaries. One
L39@P2: example was Operation Level Up, which countered crypto investment scams. This FBI-led
L40@P2: initiative has reduced potential losses by more than $500 million since 2024.
L41@P2: It has never been more important to be diligent with your cybersecurity, social media
L42@P2: footprint, and electronic interactions. Cyber threats and cyber-enabled crime will continue
L43@P2: to evolve as the world embraces emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence. At
L44@P2: the time of publication, the FBI was engaged in Operation Winter Shield, which highlights
L45@P2: concrete steps for organizations to bolster their digital security. The FBI remains fully
L46@P2: committed to ensuring Americans’ safety online and reinforcing the recent Executive Order
L47@P2: targeting cybercrime, fraud, and foreign scam centers, to hold those accountable who
L48@P2-3: exploit the internet for nefarious purposes.4 F ED ER A L BU R EAU OF I NVE STIGATIO N

L231@P10: Cyber-Enabled Fraud Trends
L232@P10: Sextortion
L233@P10: Sextortion can start on any site, app, messaging platform, or game where people meet and
L234@P10: communicate. In some cases, the first contact from the criminal will be a threat - the
L235@P10: person may claim to already have a revealing picture or video of a child that will be shared
L236@P10: if the victim does not send more pictures. More often, however, this crime starts when
L237@P10: people believe they are communicating with someone their own age who is interested in a
L238@P10: relationship, or with someone who is offering something of value. After the criminals have
L239@P10: one or more videos or pictures, they threaten to publish that content, or they threaten
L240@P10: violence, to compel the victim to produce more images. The shame, fear, and confusion
L241@P10: people feel when they are caught in this cycle often prevent them from asking for help or
L242@P10: reporting the abuse. The public should understand how sextortion occurs and openly
L243@P10: discuss online safety.
L244@P10: In 2025, IC3 received more than 75,000 submissions regarding sextortion. When
L245@P10: appropriate, IC3 refers complaints to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
L246@P10: (NCMEC). In 2025, IC3 referred more than 5,700 submissions involving minors to NCMEC.

L255@P10: Cryptocurrency Investment Fraud
L256@P10: Cryptocurrency Investment Scams are sophisticated long-term scams using
L257@P10: psychological manipulation, the appearance of legitimacy, and exploitation of
L258@P10: cryptocurrencies to deceive victims into investing large sums of money. These scams are
L259@P10: largely perpetrated by organized criminal enterprises based in Southeast Asia using
L260@P10: victims of human trafficking as forced labor to run the scam operations. Cryptocurrency
L261@P10: investment fraud was the highest source of financial losses to Americans in 2025 with $7.2
L262@P10: billion reported in losses.
L263@P10: The scammers typically initiate contact through text messages, social media sites,
L264@P10: advertisements, or dating applications and then quickly move the conversation to a
L265@P10: messaging platform. Often the victims are introduced to investment groups representing
L266@P10: themselves to be knowledgeable industry insiders offering guidance on trading or
L267@P10: investing in cryptocurrency or gold. The victims are enticed to send cryptocurrency to fake
L268@P10: investment scam platforms or apps and are shown fake profits and offered loans to
L269@P10-11: encourage larger investments. Eventually, when the victims try to withdraw their money,12 F ED ER A L BU R EAU OF I NVE STIGATIO N
L270@P11: they will be charged taxes and fees as a final attempt to exploit money from the victims
L271@P11: before the scammers disappear with all the victim funds. Victims are also targeted in
L272@P11: recovery scams, claiming to help recover lost
L273@P11: funds.
L274@P11: These scams are often devastating because they
L275@P11: can leave victims with significant financial loss and
L276@P11: emotional distress. The FBI is working to combat
L277@P11: these scams through its work on the U.S.
L278@P11: Attorney’s Office District of Columbia Scam
L279@P11: Center Strike Force and Operation Level Up, as
L280@P11: detailed in the “Positive Impact” section of this report.

L318@P12: Cyber Threats in 2025
L319@P12: Hijacked networks, cryptocurrency heists, and corporate espionage are a few examples of
L320@P12: the spiraling cyber threat. Every year, our adversaries become savvier and increasingly
L321@P12: callous – attacking power grids, shutting down hospitals, and stoking geopolitical tensions.
L322@P12: State-sponsored cyber actors wield every element of their national power to target the
L323@P12: United States and its critical infrastructure. Skilled cybercriminals exploit new and
L324@P12: longstanding vulnerabilities to steal our money and hold our data for ransom.
L325@P12: Combating these threats is the primary mission of the FBI’s Cyber program. As the lead
L326@P12: federal agency for investigating cyberattacks and intrusions, we engage with victims and
L327@P12: work to unmask those committing malicious cyber activities, wherever they are.

L374@P14: Recommendations to Protect Against Ransomware
L375@P14: A key step to limit damage and lower risk is to establish and maintain a solid foundation of
L376@P14: industry best practices, which can help mitigate the threat and reduce your organization’s
L377@P14: attack surface. The FBI recommends the following mitigating practices for companies:
L378@P14: • Create off-site or offline backups and regularly maintain backup and restoration.
L379@P14: Additionally, ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or
L380@P14: deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure.
L381@P14: • Eliminate default passwords and credentials when installing software and require all
L382@P14: accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain
L383@P14: admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s standards.
L384@P14: • Disable and remove unnecessary protocols by default. Audit user accounts with
L385@P14: administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of
L386@P14: least privilege.
L387@P14: • Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all services to the extent possible,
L388@P14: particularly for webmail, virtual private networks, and accounts that access critical
L389@P14: systems.
L390@P14: • Secure initial access points - To help in detecting the ransomware, implement a tool
L391@P14: that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a
L392@P14: network. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for
L393@P14: detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon
L394@P14: network connections for each host.
L395@P14: • Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware. Network segmentation can
L396@P14: help prevent the spread of ransomware by controlling traffic flows between—and
L397@P14: access to— various subnetworks and by restricting adversary lateral movement.
L398@P14: • Keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date. Timely patching is one
L399@P14: of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its
L400@P14: exposure to cybersecurity threats. Prioritize patching known exploited vulnerabilities in
L401@P14: internet-facing systems.
L402@P14: If you are impacted by ransomware or cybercrime, file a report with IC3 to share information
L403@P14: with the FBI.
L404@P14: For a more extensive list of mitigations and recommendations regarding ransomware, please
L405@P14-15: refer to #StopRansomware Guide | CISA.16 F ED ER A L BU R EAU OF I NVE STIGATIO N
